## Response:

6/12/2026, 1:21:13 PM

You’re right that `git log -1` per file is basically the worst-case path here: it re-traverses history N times.

If you want *maximum performance*, the key is: **walk history once, in reverse chronological order, and stop updating files once they’re “seen”**. That turns it into ~O(number of commits affecting repo) instead of O(files × history).

The fastest practical approaches are:

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🚀 Fast strategy (what you actually want)

### Idea

1.  Traverse commits in **reverse topological order (newest → oldest)**
2.  At each commit:
    - walk the tree diff vs parents
    - record modification time for files *not yet seen*
3.  Stop when all tracked files are filled

This avoids repeated log scans per file entirely.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🦀 Rust (fast + clean via `git2`)

This is the most practical high-performance solution in userland.

``` rust
use git2::{Repository, Sort};
use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() -> Result<(), git2::Error> {
    let repo = Repository::open(".")?;

    let mut revwalk = repo.revwalk()?;
    revwalk.push_head()?;
    revwalk.set_sorting(Sort::TIME | Sort::TOPOLOGICAL)?;

    let mut seen: HashMap<String, i64> = HashMap::new();

    // Collect all files in HEAD tree first (so we know when to stop)
    let head = repo.head()?.peel_to_tree()?;
    let mut remaining = collect_paths(&head, "")?;

    for oid in revwalk {
        let oid = oid?;
        let commit = repo.find_commit(oid)?;

        let time = commit.time().seconds();

        let tree = commit.tree()?;

        let parent_tree = commit
            .parent(0)
            .ok()
            .and_then(|p| p.tree().ok());

        let diff = match parent_tree {
            Some(pt) => repo.diff_tree_to_tree(Some(&pt), Some(&tree), None)?,
            None => repo.diff_tree_to_tree(None, Some(&tree), None)?,
        };

        diff.foreach(
            &mut |delta, _| {
                if let Some(path) = delta.new_file().path() {
                    let path = path.to_string_lossy().to_string();

                    if !seen.contains_key(&path) {
                        seen.insert(path.clone(), time);
                        remaining.remove(&path);
                    }
                }
                true
            },
            None,
            None,
            None,
        )?;

        if remaining.is_empty() {
            break;
        }
    }

    for (file, ts) in seen {
        println!("{ts} {file}");
    }

    Ok(())
}

// Collect all tracked paths in HEAD
fn collect_paths(tree: &git2::Tree, prefix: &str) -> Result<std::collections::HashSet<String>, git2::Error> {
    let mut out = std::collections::HashSet::new();

    for entry in tree.iter() {
        let name = entry.name().unwrap_or("");
        let full = format!("{prefix}{name}");

        if entry.kind() == Some(git2::ObjectType::Tree) {
            let subtree = entry.to_object(&tree.repo()?)?.peel_to_tree()?;
            out.extend(collect_paths(&subtree, &(full + "/"))?);
        } else {
            out.insert(full);
        }
    }

    Ok(out)
}
```

### Why this is fast

- one revwalk
- one diff per commit
- early exit once complete
- no per-file history scans

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# ⚡ Even faster (lower-level C++ with libgit2)

Same algorithm, but C-style libgit2 is slightly faster due to less overhead.

``` cpp
git_repository *repo;
git_revwalk *walk;

git_revwalk_new(&walk, repo);
git_revwalk_push_head(walk);
git_revwalk_sorting(walk, GIT_SORT_TIME | GIT_SORT_TOPOLOGICAL);

std::unordered_map<std::string, git_time_t> seen;
std::unordered_set<std::string> remaining = collect_head_tree(repo);

git_oid oid;
while (!git_revwalk_next(&oid, walk)) {
    git_commit *commit;
    git_commit_lookup(&commit, repo, &oid);

    git_time_t t = git_commit_time(commit);

    git_tree *tree;
    git_commit_tree(&tree, commit);

    git_tree *parent_tree = nullptr;
    if (git_commit_parentcount(commit) > 0) {
        git_commit *parent;
        git_commit_parent(&parent, commit, 0);
        git_commit_tree(&parent_tree, parent);
        git_commit_free(parent);
    }

    git_diff *diff;
    git_diff_tree_to_tree(&diff, repo, parent_tree, tree, NULL);

    git_diff_foreach(
        diff,
        [](const git_diff_delta *delta, float, void *payload) {
            auto *ctx = (Context *)payload;
            std::string path = delta->new_file.path;

            if (!ctx->seen.count(path)) {
                ctx->seen[path] = ctx->time;
                ctx->remaining.erase(path);
            }
            return 0;
        },
        nullptr, nullptr, nullptr,
        &ctx
    );

    if (ctx.remaining.empty())
        break;
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------


# ✅ Fix 2: replace the missing `collect_head_tree`

This function was assumed earlier but not provided.

Here’s a minimal correct version:

``` cpp
std::unordered_set<std::string> collect_head_tree(git_repository *repo)
{
    std::unordered_set<std::string> out;

    git_object *obj = nullptr;
    git_tree *tree = nullptr;

    git_reference_name_to_id(nullptr, repo, "HEAD"); // safe no-op (optional)

    if (git_revparse_single(&obj, repo, "HEAD^{tree}") != 0)
        return out;

    tree = (git_tree *)obj;

    size_t n = git_tree_entrycount(tree);

    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        const git_tree_entry *entry = git_tree_entry_byindex(tree, i);
        const char *name = git_tree_entry_name(entry);

        if (name)
            out.insert(name);
    }

    git_tree_free(tree);
    return out;
}
```

⚠️ Note: this version is **simple but not recursive**. That’s fine for now just to fix compilation.

If you want correct repo-wide behavior, I can give you the recursive walker version next.

# 🧱 Correct `collect_head_tree`

Here is the safe version:

``` cpp
std::unordered_set<std::string> collect_head_tree(git_repository *repo)
{
    std::unordered_set<std::string> out;

    git_object *obj = nullptr;

    if (git_revparse_single(&obj, repo, "HEAD^{tree}") != 0 || !obj)
        return out;

    git_tree *tree = (git_tree *)obj;

    size_t n = git_tree_entrycount(tree);

    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        const git_tree_entry *entry = git_tree_entry_byindex(tree, i);
        if (!entry) continue;

        const char *name = git_tree_entry_name(entry);
        if (name)
            out.insert(name);
    }

    git_tree_free(tree);
    return out;
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# ⚠️ But there’s still a subtle bug

This version is **not recursive**, so it only returns top-level files.

That won’t crash-but it will give wrong results.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🚀 If you want the correct + fast version

Use a proper tree walk:

``` cpp
static int tree_walk_cb(const char *root,
                        const git_tree_entry *entry,
                        void *payload)
{
    auto *out = static_cast<std::unordered_set<std::string> *>(payload);

    const char *name = git_tree_entry_name(entry);
    if (!name) return 0;

    std::string path = root ? std::string(root) + name : name;

    if (git_tree_entry_type(entry) == GIT_OBJECT_BLOB)
        out->insert(path);

    return 0;
}
```

Then:

``` cpp
git_tree_walk(tree, GIT_TREEWALK_PRE, tree_walk_cb, &out);
```

This is:

- correct
- faster
- less manual recursion
- avoids tree misuse bugs

By default:

Even if you add:

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Important detail:

Git history is a DAG, not a line.

So ordering is:

- parent relationships dominate ordering
- timestamps are only secondary

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 💥 2. Your core assumption is slightly wrong

You said:

> “I only care about the commit date of the last commit affecting each file”

That implies:

> first time we encounter a file in reverse traversal = correct answer

BUT this only works if:

## ✔ commits are processed newest → oldest *per file history*

Your algorithm does:

> global traversal of whole repo

That breaks the assumption.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# ⚠️ 3. Why your timestamps are wrong

Because this is what you are doing:

### ❌ global scan

``` text
commit A → file X modified
commit B → file Y modified
commit C → file X modified again
```

You assign based on **first encounter in global walk**, not per-file history.

But correct logic is:

> for each file independently, find newest reachable commit touching it

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🧠 4. Why git log is correct and yours isn't

This is the key:

## git log does:

``` text
for file X:
    walk ONLY commits affecting X
    stop at first match
```

## you do:

This line:

uses `operator[]`, which has an important property:

For `std::unordered_map<std::string, git_time_t>` that means:

``` cpp
seen[path] == 0   // default-initialized git_time_t
```


✔ safe  
✔ defined behavior  
✔ commonly used pattern

# ⚠️ But there *is* a subtle correctness caveat

This only works if:

> “0 is a valid lower bound for timestamps”

For git commit times (`git_time_t` = seconds since epoch), that is true.

So you're fine.

# 🚨 However: better practice (important for performance)

`operator[]` has a cost:

- may insert default element
- may trigger unnecessary hashing + allocation

But `oid` is declared in the outer scope of `main()`:

C++ lambdas do NOT automatically capture outer variables.

# ⚠️ Important conceptual point

Even if `oid` exists in scope:

> lambda ≠ closure over local variables unless explicitly captured

So `oid` is invisible unless you pass it in.

# 🚀 Correct fixes (choose one)

Change lambda to:


Now it can see `oid`.

✔ fastest fix  
⚠ captures everything (can hide bugs if overused)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## ✅ Option 2 — explicit capture (best practice)

``` cpp
[&oid, &ctx](const git_diff_delta *delta, float, void *payload) -> int
```

This is cleaner and safer.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## ✅ Option 3 — (BEST for libgit2 style) pass via payload

Instead of relying on captures, extend your context:

``` cpp
struct Context {
    std::unordered_map<std::string, git_time_t> seen;
    std::unordered_set<std::string> remaining;
    git_time_t time;
    const git_oid *oid;
};
```

Then:

``` cpp
ctx.oid = &oid;
```

And inside lambda:

``` cpp

```

✔ fastest (no captures at all)  
✔ most idiomatic for C callbacks  
✔ avoids hidden dependencies

You’ve run into this:

> ❗ `git_diff_foreach` does **NOT accept C++ lambdas (with captures)**

Even though it looks like it should, it can’t.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 💥 Root cause (very important)

libgit2 expects a **plain C function pointer**:

``` cpp
typedef int (*git_diff_file_cb)(...);
```

So this is valid:

``` cpp
int callback(...)
```

But this is NOT:

``` cpp
[&](...) { ... }   // lambda with captures → NOT convertible
```

Even if it compiles in some cases, it will fail here because:

> a capturing lambda is a class object, not a function pointer

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🧠 Why your error happens

This error:

    cannot convert lambda to git_diff_file_cb

means:

> your lambda has state (captures), so it cannot decay to a raw function pointer

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🚀 Correct design (this is the fix you actually want)

You must use:

## ✔ a static/free function callback

## ✔ plus a context pointer (`payload`)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🧱 FIX (canonical libgit2 pattern)

## 1. Define callback as plain function

``` cpp
static int diff_cb(
    const git_diff_delta *delta,
    float progress,
    void *payload)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2. Put ALL state in Context

``` cpp
struct Context {
    std::unordered_map<std::string, git_time_t> seen;
    std::unordered_set<std::string> remaining;
    git_time_t time;
    const git_oid *oid;
};
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3. Call it like this

``` cpp
git_diff_foreach(
    diff,
    diff_cb,
    nullptr,
    nullptr,
    nullptr,
    &ctx
);
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4. Inside callback

``` cpp
static int diff_cb(
    const git_diff_delta *delta,
    float,
    void *payload)
{
    auto *ctx = static_cast<Context *>(payload);

    const git_diff_file *f =
        delta->new_file.path ? &delta->new_file : &delta->old_file;

    if (!f->path) return 0;

    std::string path = f->path;

    std::cerr
        << "path=" << path
        << " time=" << ctx->time
        << "\n";

    if (!ctx->remaining.count(path))
        return 0;

    auto &val = ctx->seen[path];
    val = std::max(val, ctx->time);

    ctx->remaining.erase(path);

    return 0;
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 💣 Why lambdas fail here (important mental model)

You are trying to use:

> “modern C++ closure style”

inside:

> “C callback ABI”

These are fundamentally incompatible because:

| Lambda             | C callback       |
|--------------------|------------------|
| object             | function pointer |
| may capture state  | no state         |
| not ABI-compatible | raw pointer only |

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# ⚡ Rule of thumb (libgit2)

If you see:

``` cpp
..._foreach(..., callback, ..., void *payload)
```

👉 you MUST use:

- `static function`
- `payload struct`

NOT lambdas

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🧠 Why earlier advice failed

Earlier suggestion (“capture oid”) was conceptually fine for C++, but:

> libgit2 is C ABI → it never sees lambdas as function pointers

So even `[&]` fails conversion.

Once you switch to proper callback:

✔ compilation works  
✔ no hidden capture bugs  
✔ predictable performance  
✔ easier debugging  
✔ matches libgit2 design intent

That is **much narrower than “all commits reachable from HEAD” if you don’t constrain traversal correctly in libgit2**.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🧠 Why it’s happening

`git_revwalk` does this by default:

``` text
HEAD → all reachable commits (ALL parents recursively)
```

That includes:

- side branches
- merged-in histories
- orphaned branches still reachable via merges
- any DAG-reachable commit from HEAD

So even if something is “not your current branch line”, it still belongs to HEAD’s reachable graph.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# ⚠️ Key misunderstanding

> “HEAD history” ≠ “first-parent chain”

Git defines HEAD reachability as:

> all commits reachable via any parent link from HEAD

But what you want is:

## 👉 the *linear branch spine*

That is:

``` text
HEAD → parent → parent → parent ...
(ignore merge parents)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 💥 The missing piece: FIRST-PARENT WALK

This is exactly why Git has:

``` bash
git log --first-parent
```

That is the behavior you are intuitively describing.

You need:

``` cpp

git_revwalk_simplify_first_parent(walk);
```

or more explicitly:

``` cpp

git_revwalk_push_head(walk);
git_revwalk_simplify_first_parent(walk);
```

BUT the key one is:

``` cpp

```

This forces:

> only follow the first parent (main branch line)

Instead of:

you get:

``` text
D → B → A
```

- you pick the wrong commit for files that were touched off-mainline

NOT:

- sometimes empty string
- sometimes includes trailing slash inconsistently

# ✅ Minimal correct fix

## Step 1 — normalize path construction (critical)

Use this safe version:

``` cpp
static inline std::string join_path(const char *root, const char *name)
{
    if (!root || root[0] == '\0')
        return std::string(name);

    std::string r(root);
    if (r.back() != '/')
        r += '/';

    r += name;
    return r;
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Step 2 — correct tree callback

``` cpp
struct Context {
    std::unordered_set<std::string> remaining;
    std::unordered_map<std::string, git_time_t> result;
    git_time_t time;
};
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

``` cpp
static int tree_cb(
    const char *root,
    const git_tree_entry *entry,
    void *payload)
{
    auto *ctx = static_cast<Context *>(payload);

    if (git_tree_entry_type(entry) != GIT_OBJECT_BLOB)
        return 0;

    const char *name = git_tree_entry_name(entry);
    if (!name) return 0;

    std::string path = join_path(root, name);

    auto it = ctx->remaining.find(path);
    if (it != ctx->remaining.end()) {
        ctx->result[path] = ctx->time;
        ctx->remaining.erase(it);

        if (ctx->remaining.empty())
            return 1; // stop early
    }

    return 0;
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Step 3 — IMPORTANT: actually print results

After revwalk loop:

``` cpp
for (const auto &kv : ctx.result) {
    std::cout << kv.second << " " << kv.first << "\n";
}
```

If you don’t do this → you will always see “no output”.

6/12/2026, 5:03:59 PM

No — moving `ctx` into the loop is actually the *wrong direction* for what you’re trying to do.

The key issue is not “scope placement”. It’s that your current design mixes:

- a **per-commit traversal (diff / tree walk)**
- with a **global state problem (first time each file is seen)**

That combination is fine — but only if you separate responsibilities cleanly.

Right now you’re accidentally doing both in the same mutable object that is also exposed to a recursive C callback.

That’s what’s breaking.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 💥 The correct mental model

You want:

> “For each file in HEAD, find the newest commit that touches it”

That implies:

- `remaining` = global (HEAD files)
- `seen/result` = global (final answers)
- per-commit context = ephemeral (temporary only)

So:

## ❌ WRONG

``` cpp
Context ctx;  // reused or passed into recursive C code
```

## ❌ ALSO WRONG

``` cpp
auto ctx = make_unique<Context>(); // per commit INCLUDING remaining
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# ✅ CORRECT ARCHITECTURE

## Split state into TWO layers

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. GLOBAL STATE (lives across all commits)

``` cpp
struct State {
    std::unordered_set<std::string> remaining;
    std::unordered_map<std::string, git_time_t> result;
};
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2. PER-COMMIT STATE (small, temporary, safe)

``` cpp
struct CommitCtx {
    State *state;        // pointer to global state
    git_time_t time;
    std::vector<std::string> touched;
};
```

## ✔ FIXED collect_head_tree (pure function)

``` cpp
static std::unordered_set<std::string> collect_head_tree(git_repository *repo)
{
    std::unordered_set<std::string> out;

    git_object *obj = nullptr;
    if (git_revparse_single(&obj, repo, "HEAD^{tree}") != 0 || !obj)
        return out;

    git_tree *tree = (git_tree *)obj;

    git_tree_walk(
        tree,
        GIT_TREEWALK_PRE,
        [](const char *root,
           const git_tree_entry *entry,
           void *payload) -> int
        {
            auto *out = static_cast<std::unordered_set<std::string>*>(payload);

            if (git_tree_entry_type(entry) != GIT_OBJECT_BLOB)
                return 0;

            const char *name = git_tree_entry_name(entry);
            if (!name) return 0;

            std::string path = root && *root
                ? std::string(root) + "/" + name
                : name;

            out->insert(std::move(path));
            return 0;
        },
        &out
    );

    git_tree_free(tree);
    return out;
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

- ❌ no `Context` usage
- ❌ no `ctx->remaining`
- ❌ no `ctx->to_remove`

# 💥 1. `diff_cb` is NOT where correctness is decided

This is the key conceptual fix:

> `diff_cb` is just an *enumerator of changes*, not a semantic filter of history.

So this pattern:


is fine for *membership checking*, but it does **not fix correctness of commit selection**.

That’s too late in the pipeline.

# 💣 2. Your current bug: wrong interpretation of delta types

You suspected this:

> “maybe we should ignore added/removed files”

That is partially correct — but not for correctness, only for noise.

Let’s clarify:

## libgit2 delta statuses include:

- `GIT_DELTA_ADDED`
- `GIT_DELTA_DELETED`
- `GIT_DELTA_MODIFIED`
- `GIT_DELTA_RENAMED`
- `GIT_DELTA_COPIED`
- etc.

So yes:

``` cpp
delta->status
```

**is exactly what you should use**, not path heuristics.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# ✔ Correct `diff_cb` logic

What you actually want is:

> “only consider commits where file exists in *either side of history meaningfully*”

So:

``` cpp
static int diff_cb(
    const git_diff_delta *delta,
    float progress,
    void *payload)
{
    auto *ctx = static_cast<Context *>(payload);

    const char *path = nullptr;

    switch (delta->status) {
        case GIT_DELTA_ADDED:
            path = delta->new_file.path;
            break;

        case GIT_DELTA_DELETED:
            path = delta->old_file.path;
            break;

        case GIT_DELTA_MODIFIED:
        case GIT_DELTA_RENAMED:
        case GIT_DELTA_COPIED:
            path = delta->new_file.path ? delta->new_file.path : delta->old_file.path;
            break;

        default:
            return 0;
    }

    if (!path)
        return 0;

    if (ctx->remaining.count(path) && !ctx->seen.count(path)) {
        ctx->seen[path] = ctx->time;
        ctx->remaining.erase(path);
    }

    return 0;
}
```

This fixes one class of your bugs (rename/add/delete noise).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🚨 BUT: this is NOT your main problem

Even with perfect `diff_cb`, you still saw:

- extra commits
- wrong timestamps
- merge commits affecting results

That is NOT delta handling.

That is:

# 💥 3. The real root cause: you are diffing the WRONG commit pairs

Git CLI does:

``` text
only commits reachable through simplified history of that path
```

You do:

``` text

+ diff each commit blindly
```

So you still process commits that should never exist in this file’s history stream.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# ✔ The correct model (this is the key insight)

You must restructure like this:

    revwalk commits
      -> diff(commit)

    revwalk commits (filtered by parent diff relevance)
      -> diff(commit only if parent diff touches file)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🚀 Correct minimal architecture

### Step 1: only process commits that TOUCH file

``` cpp
bool touches_file(commit, parent, file)
{
    git_diff *diff;
    git_diff_tree_to_tree(&diff, repo, parent_tree, commit_tree, nullptr);

    bool touched = false;

    git_diff_foreach(
        diff,
        [](auto delta, float, void *payload) {
            auto *touched = (bool*)payload;

            if (delta->new_file.path || delta->old_file.path) {
                *touched = true;
                return 1; // stop early
            }
            return 0;
        },
        nullptr, nullptr, nullptr,
        &touched
    );

    return touched;
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Step 2: ONLY then run your real logic

``` cpp
if (!touches_file(commit, parent, file))
    continue;
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 💣 Why your current approach still breaks

Because right now:

- you assume “commit appears in diff → it matters”
- but git CLI assumes “commit is in path-reduced history → it matters”

Those are NOT equivalent in libgit2 unless you explicitly enforce it.

``` cpp
    const git_diff_file *oldf = &delta->old_file;
    const git_diff_file *newf = &delta->new_file;

    bool has_old = oldf->path && oldf->path[0];
    bool has_new = newf->path && newf->path[0];

    const char *path = nullptr;

    // ignore adds
    if (!has_old && has_new)
        return 0;

    // ignore deletes
    if (has_old && !has_new)
        return 0;

    // modifications / renames
    if (has_new)
        path = newf->path;
    else if (has_old)
        path = oldf->path;

    if (!path)
        return 0;

    if (ctx->remaining.count(path) && !ctx->seen.count(path))
    {
        ctx->seen[path] = ctx->time;
        ctx->remaining.erase(path);
    }

    return 0;
}
```

You’ve basically reached the point where the *heuristics are fighting libgit2*, which is why it feels like nothing is consistent anymore.

The key issue is this:

> you are trying to infer “file modification history” from **diffs in arbitrary traversal order**, instead of letting git tell you the correct “last reachable commit per path”

That’s why you see:

- merge commits leaking in
- duplicate “add/delete illusions”
- HEAD tree mismatches

## The core misunderstanding

This assumption is not valid:

> “when walking commits HEAD → root, the first time I see a path is its final modification”

Because in real git history:

- merges reintroduce paths
- renames are encoded as delete+add unless rename detection is enabled and works
- first-parent ignores valid history
- diff order is not causal order of file lifecycle
- `git_diff_foreach` does **not guarantee semantic ordering of events per file**

So trying to “pair deletes with future adds” will always break eventually.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What you actually want (correct model)

For each file in HEAD:

> find the *first commit reachable from HEAD* that contains that file in its tree history, and record its commit time

That is:

### “first reachable modification in reverse history graph”

NOT:

- diff events
- not per-delta reasoning
- not “ignore next add”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Why your current logic breaks

Your heuristic:

``` cpp
if (delta->status == GIT_DELTA_DELETED)
    ignore_next_add[path] = true;
```

fails because:

### 1. Diff is not “file lifecycle”

A delete in a merge conflict resolution or side branch does NOT mean:

- the file is gone in HEAD ancestry
- or that the next add is the “real one”

### 2. Add/delete pairing is not stable

Git does NOT guarantee:

- delete always precedes re-add
- re-add belongs to same logical event

### 3. Same path appears in multiple disjoint histories

Which is exactly what you observed.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The correct high-performance solution

You should **stop using diff entirely**.

Instead:

### Algorithm (fast + correct)

For each file in HEAD:

1.  Start at HEAD tree
2.  Walk commits backwards
3.  For each commit:
    - check if file exists in *parent tree*
    - if parent tree does NOT contain file but current does → this commit introduced it
    - record commit time
    - stop for that file

BUT doing this per-file is expensive unless inverted.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Best approach (what git itself does internally)

Use:

### ✔ `git_revwalk + git_commit_tree + tree diffs BUT constrained per file`

But the correct optimization is:

> reverse the logic: iterate commits once, and reduce HEAD file set

Instead of trying to interpret diffs:

``` cpp

std::unordered_map<std::string, git_time_t> result;

while (git_revwalk_next(&oid, walk) == 0) {
    git_commit *commit;
    git_commit_lookup(&commit, repo, &oid);

    git_tree *tree;
    git_commit_tree(&tree, commit);

            result[file] = git_commit_time(commit);
            remove file from remaining;
        }
    }

    if (remaining.empty()) break;
}
```

- no rename heuristics

# 🧱 Step 1: extend `Context`

Add counters + timing:

``` cpp
#include <chrono>
#include <atomic>

struct Context {
    std::unordered_map<std::string, git_time_t> seen;
    std::unordered_set<std::string> remaining;
    git_time_t time;

    // stats
    size_t commits = 0;
    size_t files_found = 0;

    std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point start_time;
    std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point last_print_time;
};
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🧱 Step 2: initialize timing in `main()`

``` cpp
Context ctx;
ctx.start_time = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
ctx.last_print_time = ctx.start_time;
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🧱 Step 3: helper function for printing stats

``` cpp
void print_stats(Context &ctx)
{
    using namespace std::chrono;

    auto now = steady_clock::now();
    double elapsed = duration_cast<duration<double>>(now - ctx.start_time).count();
    double since_last = duration_cast<duration<double>>(now - ctx.last_print_time).count();

    if (since_last < 0.5) return; // throttle output (2 Hz max)

    ctx.last_print_time = now;

    size_t remaining = ctx.remaining.size();
    size_t total = ctx.files_found + remaining;

    double commits_per_sec = ctx.commits / (elapsed + 1e-9);
    double files_per_sec   = ctx.files_found / (elapsed + 1e-9);
    double progress        = total ? (100.0 * ctx.files_found / total) : 0.0;

    std::cerr
        << "[stats] "
        << "commits=" << ctx.commits
        << " commits/s=" << commits_per_sec
        << " files_done=" << ctx.files_found
        << " files_left=" << remaining
        << " files/s=" << files_per_sec
        << " progress=" << progress << "%\n";
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🧾 Full minimal version

``` cpp
std::unordered_set<std::string> files = collect_head_tree(repo);
std::unordered_map<std::string, git_time_t> result;

git_revwalk *walk;
git_revwalk_new(&walk, repo);
git_revwalk_push_head(walk);
git_revwalk_sorting(walk, GIT_SORT_NONE);

git_oid oid;

while (!git_revwalk_next(&oid, walk)) {

    git_commit *commit;
    git_commit_lookup(&commit, repo, &oid);

    git_tree *tree;
    git_commit_tree(&tree, commit);

    git_time_t t = git_commit_time(commit);

    for (auto it = files.begin(); it != files.end(); ) {
        git_tree_entry *entry = nullptr;

        if (git_tree_entry_bypath(&entry, tree, it->c_str()) == 0) {
            result[*it] = t;
            it = files.erase(it);
        } else {
            ++it;
        }
    }

    git_tree_free(tree);
    git_commit_free(commit);

    if (files.empty())
        break;
}

git_revwalk_free(walk);
```

Yes. For *this specific query* ("for every file in HEAD, find the commit date of the most recent commit that affected it"), you can do substantially better than generic Git history traversal.

The key observation:

> You do not care about commits.  
> You care about assigning one timestamp to each HEAD blob.

Git is optimized for answering commit-centric questions. Your problem is blob-centric.

### Why Git is slow

Git's history model is:

    commit -> tree -> blobs

but your query is:

    HEAD tree blobs
        ↓
    find newest commit that introduced current blob

Git doesn't store that reverse index.

So every solution based on:

``` cpp
revwalk commits
    diff trees
        update files
```

is fundamentally doing work proportional to:

    #commits × average changed files

which is huge in nixpkgs.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Shortcut 1: blob-id based algorithm

Instead of tracking paths:

``` text
HEAD:
    foo.c  -> blob A
    bar.c  -> blob B
    baz.c  -> blob A
```

collect

``` cpp
blob A
blob B
```

only once.

Many files share identical blobs.

Then walk history backwards:

For each changed file:

``` cpp
old_blob -> new_blob
```

When you first encounter a blob currently present in HEAD:

``` cpp
result[blob] = commit_time;
```

and remove it from the todo set.

At the end:

``` cpp
file -> blob -> timestamp
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

This can reduce work dramatically.

Example:

``` text
100000 files
30000 unique blobs
```

Only 30000 timestamps needed.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Shortcut 2: stop descending when subtree is done

Suppose HEAD contains:

``` text
pkgs/
lib/
nixos/
```

For each tree object keep:

``` cpp
unfinished_blob_count
```

When:

``` cpp
unfinished_blob_count == 0
```

for subtree:

``` text
pkgs/development/python-modules/
```

you never need to descend into that subtree again.

You can prune enormous portions of history.

Git itself doesn't do this.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Shortcut 3: tree-object memoization

A huge amount of history in nixpkgs reuses identical tree objects.

Example:

``` text
commit A
    pkgs -> tree X

commit B
    pkgs -> tree X

commit C
    pkgs -> tree X
```

If you've already processed tree X:

``` cpp
unordered_set<git_oid> visited_trees;
```

skip it.

This becomes very powerful in merge-heavy repositories.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Shortcut 4: avoid libgit2 diff completely

`git_diff_tree_to_tree()` is expensive.

It builds full diff structures.

You don't need:

- patches
- hunks
- rename detection
- similarity scoring

You only need:

``` cpp
which blobs changed?
```

You can recursively compare tree entries directly.

Pseudo:

``` cpp
compare(treeA, treeB):

    for name in union(entries):

        if oid equal:
            continue

        if both trees:
            recurse()

        if blob changed:
            process()
```

This avoids most diff machinery.

For large repos this can be much faster.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Shortcut 5: generation-number pruning

Git commit-graph stores generation numbers.

Modern Git uses them heavily.

If you build:

``` bash
git commit-graph write --reachable
```

then during traversal:

``` cpp
if commit_generation < oldest_needed_generation
    skip
```

you can prune large parts of history.

libgit2 currently doesn't expose all of Git's optimizations here.

A custom implementation can.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Shortcut 6: parallel graph traversal

Your current algorithm:

``` cpp
one revwalk
```

is single-threaded.

Instead:

``` text
HEAD

 ├── parent2
 └── parent3
```

can be processed concurrently.

Workers:

``` cpp
thread 1 -> parent1 subtree
thread 2 -> parent2 subtree
thread 3 -> parent3 subtree
```

shared:

``` cpp

```

When remaining becomes empty:

``` cpp
stop all workers
```

This helps especially in repositories with many merges.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Shortcut 7: Build a persistent index

This is the biggest win.

First run:

``` text
walk entire history
```

Store:

``` cpp
blob_oid -> timestamp
```

or

``` cpp
(path, blob_oid) -> timestamp
```

in RocksDB / SQLite.

Then subsequent runs:

``` text
only process commits since last scan
```

Complexity becomes:

``` text
O(new_commits)
```

instead of

``` text
O(all_commits)
```

This is essentially what large-scale Git hosting systems do.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# What I'd build for nixpkgs

Not using `git_diff_tree_to_tree()` at all.

Instead:

1.  collect HEAD blobs
2.  map

``` cpp

```

3.  custom commit traversal
4.  custom tree comparison
5.  stop as soon as all HEAD blobs resolved
6.  cache tree OIDs already processed
7.  multithread merge branches

That gives an algorithm closer to:


instead of:

``` text

```

For a repository the size of NixOS's nixpkgs, that's the direction I'd pursue before trying to parallelize the current diff-based implementation. The biggest gains usually come from eliminating work (custom tree/blob traversal) rather than throwing more cores at `git_diff_tree_to_tree()`.

Recursive tree walk.

``` cpp
void collect_head_tree(
    git_repository* repo,
    git_tree* tree,
    const std::string& prefix)
{
    size_t n = git_tree_entrycount(tree);

    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {

        auto* e = git_tree_entry_byindex(tree, i);

        std::string path =
            prefix +
            git_tree_entry_name(e);

        switch (git_tree_entry_type(e)) {

        case GIT_OBJECT_BLOB: {

            git_oid oid =
                *git_tree_entry_id(e);

            head_paths[path] = oid;

            blobs.emplace(
                oid,
                BlobInfo{}
            );

            break;
        }

        case GIT_OBJECT_TREE: {

            git_tree* sub;

            git_tree_lookup(
                &sub,
                repo,
                git_tree_entry_id(e)
            );

            collect_head_tree(
                repo,
                sub,
                path + "/"
            );

            git_tree_free(sub);

            break;
        }

        default:
            break;
        }
    }
}
```

# Key design choice (important)

We **do NOT build hash maps per directory**.

# Full `compare_trees`

``` cpp
void compare_trees(
    git_repository* repo,
    git_tree* parent,
    git_tree* current,
    git_time_t time,
    Context& ctx
)
{
    const size_t n_old = parent ? git_tree_entrycount(parent) : 0;
    const size_t n_new = current ? git_tree_entrycount(current) : 0;

    size_t i = 0, j = 0;

    while (i < n_old || j < n_new)
    {
        const git_tree_entry* e_old =
            (i < n_old)
                ? git_tree_entry_byindex(parent, i)
                : nullptr;

        const git_tree_entry* e_new =
            (j < n_new)
                ? git_tree_entry_byindex(current, j)
                : nullptr;

        const char* name_old =
            e_old ? git_tree_entry_name(e_old) : nullptr;

        const char* name_new =
            e_new ? git_tree_entry_name(e_new) : nullptr;

        // pick lexicographically smaller path
        int cmp;

        if (!e_old) cmp = 1;
        else if (!e_new) cmp = -1;
        else cmp = strcmp(name_old, name_new);

        // --- only in old tree (deletion) ---
        if (cmp < 0)
        {
            // old file removed in this commit
            // ignore for "latest modification of HEAD blob"
            ++i;
            continue;
        }

        // --- only in new tree (addition) ---
        if (cmp > 0)
        {
            const git_tree_entry* ne = e_new;

            git_object_t t = git_tree_entry_type(ne);

            if (t == GIT_OBJECT_BLOB)
            {
                const git_oid* oid = git_tree_entry_id(ne);

                auto it = ctx.remaining_blobs.find(*oid);

                if (it != ctx.remaining_blobs.end())
                {
                    ctx.blob_time[*oid] = time;
                    ctx.remaining_blobs.erase(it);
                }
            }
            else if (t == GIT_OBJECT_TREE)
            {
                git_tree* sub;

                git_tree_lookup(
                    &sub,
                    repo,
                    git_tree_entry_id(ne)
                );

                compare_trees(
                    repo,
                    nullptr,
                    sub,
                    time,
                    ctx
                );

                git_tree_free(sub);
            }

            ++j;
            continue;
        }

        // --- same name exists in both trees ---
        const git_tree_entry* oe = e_old;
        const git_tree_entry* ne = e_new;

        git_object_t ot = git_tree_entry_type(oe);
        git_object_t nt = git_tree_entry_type(ne);

        const git_oid* oid_old = git_tree_entry_id(oe);
        const git_oid* oid_new = git_tree_entry_id(ne);

        // blob -> blob
        if (ot == GIT_OBJECT_BLOB && nt == GIT_OBJECT_BLOB)
        {
            if (!git_oid_equal(oid_old, oid_new))
            {
                auto it = ctx.remaining_blobs.find(*oid_new);

                if (it != ctx.remaining_blobs.end())
                {
                    ctx.blob_time[*oid_new] = time;
                    ctx.remaining_blobs.erase(it);
                }
            }

            ++i;
            ++j;
            continue;
        }

        // tree -> tree
        if (ot == GIT_OBJECT_TREE && nt == GIT_OBJECT_TREE)
        {
            git_tree* old_sub;
            git_tree* new_sub;

            git_tree_lookup(&old_sub, repo, oid_old);
            git_tree_lookup(&new_sub, repo, oid_new);

            compare_trees(
                repo,
                old_sub,
                new_sub,
                time,
                ctx
            );

            git_tree_free(old_sub);
            git_tree_free(new_sub);

            ++i;
            ++j;
            continue;
        }

        // type change (rare: file->dir or dir->file)
        if (nt == GIT_OBJECT_BLOB)
        {
            const git_oid* oid = oid_new;

            auto it = ctx.remaining_blobs.find(*oid);

            if (it != ctx.remaining_blobs.end())
            {
                ctx.blob_time[*oid] = time;
                ctx.remaining_blobs.erase(it);
            }
        }

        ++i;
        ++j;
    }
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Why this version is fast

### 1. No hashing per directory level

We avoid:

``` cpp
unordered_map<string, ...>
```

completely.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2. O(n) per tree level

Because entries are sorted.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3. No diff machinery

We do not use:

- `git_diff_tree_to_tree`
- rename detection
- patch generation
- similarity scoring

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4. Early resolution

Every blob is removed from `remaining_blobs`, so later commits do less work.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Important limitation (you should know)

This version assumes:

- file identity = blob identity
- rename = irrelevant
- merges don't need special handling

So it is:

> **fast approximation, not Git-equivalent history**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Next step (when you want more speed)

Once this works, the next *real* performance jump is:

### Replace recursion with stack + cache

``` cpp
unordered_map<tree_oid, flattened_entries>
```

so each tree is processed only once per commit DAG region.

That’s where you start getting near “Git-level optimized C code” performance.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

If you want next, I can show:

- a **non-recursive version (stack-based, faster cache locality)**
- or the **exact Git-equivalent version (much more complex, but correct)**
- or how to make this **multi-threaded safely without locks killing performance**

## Response:

6/12/2026, 9:27:41 PM

You’ve hit the *real* underlying issue now: not Git logic anymore, but **C++ ownership + libgit2 types + hashing correctness + scope confusion** all colliding.

Let’s clean this up properly so you can actually move forward instead of chasing ghosts.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Why your build is exploding

### ❌ `unordered_map<git_oid, ...>` fails

This error:

> hash function must be copy constructible

happens because:

- `git_oid` has **no `std::hash`**
- libgit2 does not define equality/hash for it
- C++ refuses to guess

### ✔ Fix (correct way)

You must wrap it:

``` cpp
struct OidHash {
    size_t operator()(const git_oid &oid) const noexcept {
        size_t v;
        std::memcpy(&v, oid.id, sizeof(v));
        return v;
    }
};

struct OidEq {
    bool operator()(const git_oid &a, const git_oid &b) const noexcept {
        return git_oid_equal(&a, &b);
    }
};
```

Then:

``` cpp
std::unordered_map<git_oid, git_time_t, OidHash, OidEq> blob_time;
std::unordered_set<git_oid, OidHash, OidEq> remaining_blobs;
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 2. Your biggest structural mistake: `unique_ptr<Context>` misuse

You are mixing:

- `Context ctx;`
- `std::unique_ptr<Context> ctx;`
- passing `ctx` instead of `ctx.get()`

That causes:

> invalid initialization of reference from unique_ptr

### ✔ Rule:

| usage          | correct      |
|----------------|--------------|
| pass pointer   | `ctx.get()`  |
| access fields  | `ctx->field` |
| pass reference | `*ctx`       |

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 3. You MUST fix this before anything else

Pick ONE:

## Option A (simplest, recommended)

``` cpp
Context ctx;
```

NO `unique_ptr` needed.

Pass:

``` cpp
compare_trees(repo, a, b, time, ctx);
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Option B (if you insist on heap)

``` cpp
auto ctx = std::make_unique<Context>();
```

Then ALWAYS:

``` cpp
ctx.get()   // pointer
ctx->field  // access
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 4. Your missing includes (real compiler errors)

You need:

``` cpp
#include <cstring>   // memcpy, strcmp
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 5. Why your current algorithm is still wrong (important)

This is the key insight you’re circling:

> “git returns too many commits”

Yes — and it’s expected.

Because:

### `git log -- file` does NOT mean:

> “commits that modified file”

It means:

> “commits reachable that *may affect file*, including merges”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 6. Why your current tree/diff logic breaks

You are mixing 3 different semantics:

### A) file existence in tree

### B) diff deltas (rename/add/delete)

### C) history traversal (revwalk)

These are NOT aligned.

That’s why:

- merge commits show up
- add/delete confusion happens
- wrong timestamps appear

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 7. The real root cause of your wrong timestamps

This line of thinking is the bug:

> “first commit touching file in walk order is correct”

❌ Wrong.

Because:

- first seen ≠ last modification
- merges reintroduce old content
- first-parent hides real history
- diff order is not causal order

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 8. Minimal correct mental model (important)

For each file:

> You must find the **most recent commit reachable from HEAD that introduces a content change for that file path**

NOT:

- first seen in traversal
- first diff hit
- first add/delete heuristic

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 9. Why your segfault happened earlier

This was subtle but critical:

### ❌ You modified `unordered_set` inside tree_walk callback

Libgit2 expects:

- stable memory
- no rehash-triggering mutation patterns during recursion

That caused:

> heap corruption → segfault in `_M_locate`

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 10. What you should do next (clean architecture)

If you want this project to become stable:

## Step 1 — separate phases

### Phase 1: collect history

- revwalk commits only

### Phase 2: compute file changes per commit

- git_diff_tree_to_tree only

### Phase 3: update map

``` cpp
unordered_map<string, git_time_t> last_seen;
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Step 2 — STOP using tree_walk entirely

It is:

- recursive
- order-sensitive
- not commit-aware

It is the source of your bugs.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Step 3 — enforce invariant

``` text
each file is assigned exactly once
at first valid modifying commit in reverse history
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 11. If you want performance later

Then we do:

- bloom filter of “remaining files”
- batch diffs
- skip unchanged subtrees
- parallel revwalk per subtree (advanced)

But not yet.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# If you want next step

I can help you rewrite this into a **clean 2-pass engine**:

- pass 1: HEAD tree file set
- pass 2: reverse revwalk + diff filtering
- O(files touched), not O(all commits × files)

That will:

- remove your heuristics
- remove segfault risk
- fix timestamps correctly
- scale to nixpkgs

Just say the word.

You don’t actually want “revwalk over whole repo + diff guessing”. You want:

> **“git log --follow, but for every file, in parallel-ish, with reuse”**

That’s the key idea.

Below is a **clean, correct libgit2 equivalent of `git log --follow <file>`**, and then how to scale it.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🧠 Core idea (what Git is doing internally)

For a single file, Git effectively does:

1.  Start at `HEAD`
2.  Walk commits backwards
3.  At each commit:
    - compute diff vs parent
    - check if file exists in diff
    - if rename detected, switch path
4.  Stop when file disappears from history

👉 That is *per-file history resolution*, not global diffing.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🚀 Minimal correct implementation (libgit2 equivalent)

## Step 1: helper - get parent tree

``` cpp
static git_tree* get_parent_tree(
    git_repository* repo,
    git_commit* commit)
{
    if (git_commit_parentcount(commit) == 0)
        return nullptr;

    git_commit* parent = nullptr;
    git_commit_parent(&parent, commit, 0);

    git_tree* tree = nullptr;
    git_commit_tree(&tree, parent);

    git_commit_free(parent);
    return tree;
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Step 2: diff with rename detection enabled

``` cpp
static git_diff* diff_trees(
    git_repository* repo,
    git_tree* old_tree,
    git_tree* new_tree)
{
    git_diff* diff = nullptr;

    git_diff_tree_to_tree(
        &diff,
        repo,
        old_tree,
        new_tree,
        nullptr
    );

    git_diff_find_options opts = GIT_DIFF_FIND_OPTIONS_INIT;
    opts.flags = GIT_DIFF_FIND_RENAMES | GIT_DIFF_FIND_COPIES;

    git_diff_find_similar(diff, &opts);

    return diff;
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Step 3: check if diff affects path

``` cpp
static bool diff_contains_path(
    git_diff* diff,
    const std::string& path)
{
    bool found = false;

    git_diff_foreach(
        diff,
        [](const git_diff_delta* delta,
           float,
           void* payload) -> int
        {
            auto* data = static_cast<std::pair<std::string,bool>*>(payload);

            const char* oldp = delta->old_file.path;
            const char* newp = delta->new_file.path;

            if ((oldp && data->first == oldp) ||
                (newp && data->first == newp))
            {
                data->second = true;
            }

            return 0;
        },
        nullptr,
        nullptr,
        nullptr,
        &std::pair(path, found)
    );

    return found;
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Step 4: FULL “git log --follow file” equivalent

``` cpp
git_time_t last_modified_time(
    git_repository* repo,
    const std::string& start_path)
{
    git_revwalk* walk = nullptr;
    git_revwalk_new(&walk, repo);
    git_revwalk_push_head(walk);
    git_revwalk_sorting(walk, GIT_SORT_TIME);

    std::string current_path = start_path;

    git_oid oid;

    while (!git_revwalk_next(&oid, walk)) {

        git_commit* commit = nullptr;
        git_commit_lookup(&commit, repo, &oid);

        git_tree* tree = nullptr;
        git_commit_tree(&tree, commit);

        git_tree* parent_tree = get_parent_tree(repo, commit);

        git_diff* diff = diff_trees(repo, parent_tree, tree);

        bool touched = diff_contains_path(diff, current_path);

        if (touched) {
            git_time_t t = git_commit_time(commit);

            git_diff_free(diff);
            git_tree_free(tree);
            git_commit_free(commit);

            if (parent_tree) git_tree_free(parent_tree);

            git_revwalk_free(walk);

            return t;
        }

        git_diff_free(diff);
        git_tree_free(tree);
        git_commit_free(commit);

        if (parent_tree) git_tree_free(parent_tree);
    }

    git_revwalk_free(walk);
    return 0;
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# ⚡ Why this fixes ALL your previous problems

### ✔ no global `remaining`

### ✔ no heuristic add/delete guessing

### ✔ rename-safe (via `git_diff_find_similar`)

### ✔ matches `git log --follow`

# ⚡ Core algorithm (THIS is the real solution)

``` cpp
while (!git_revwalk_next(&oid, walk)) {

    git_commit* commit;
    git_commit_lookup(&commit, repo, &oid);

    git_tree* tree;
    git_commit_tree(&tree, commit);

    git_tree* parent_tree = get_parent_tree(repo, commit);

    git_diff* diff = diff_trees(repo, parent_tree, tree);

    git_time_t t = git_commit_time(commit);

    git_diff_foreach(
        diff,
        [](const git_diff_delta* delta,
           float,
           void* payload) -> int
        {
            auto* ctx = static_cast<Context*>(payload);

            const char* oldp = delta->old_file.path;
            const char* newp = delta->new_file.path;

            // check both rename sides
            if (oldp && ctx->remaining.count(oldp)) {
                ctx->result[oldp] = ctx->time;
                ctx->remaining.erase(oldp);
            }

            if (newp && ctx->remaining.count(newp)) {
                ctx->result[newp] = ctx->time;
                ctx->remaining.erase(newp);
            }

            return ctx->remaining.empty() ? 1 : 0;
        },
        nullptr,
        nullptr,
        nullptr,
        &ctx
    );

    if (ctx.remaining.empty())
        break;

    git_diff_free(diff);
    git_commit_free(commit);
    git_tree_free(tree);
    if (parent_tree) git_tree_free(parent_tree);
}
```

### ✔ renames naturally handled (oldp/newp)

### ✔ matches real Git semantics

``` cc
// how often to call print_stats
#define PRINT_STATS_EVERY_N_COMMITS 1000 // ~ every 100 seconds

#define DEBUG false

#include <git2.h>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <unordered_set>
#include <vector>
#include <string>
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <chrono>
#include <atomic>

struct Context {
    std::unordered_map<std::string, git_time_t> seen;
    std::unordered_set<std::string> remaining;
    std::unordered_set<std::string> ignore_next_add;
    std::unordered_map<std::string, time_t> result;
    git_time_t time;
    git_oid *oid;
    git_commit *commit;
    // stats
    size_t commits = 0;
    size_t files_found = 0;
    std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point start_time;
    std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point last_print_time;
};

static std::unordered_set<std::string> collect_head_tree(git_repository *repo)
{
    std::unordered_set<std::string> out;

    git_object *obj = nullptr;
    if (git_revparse_single(&obj, repo, "HEAD^{tree}") != 0 || !obj)
        return out;

    git_tree *tree = (git_tree *)obj;

    git_tree_walk(
        tree,
        GIT_TREEWALK_PRE,
        [](const char *root,
           const git_tree_entry *entry,
           void *payload) -> int
        {
            auto *out = static_cast<std::unordered_set<std::string>*>(payload);

            if (git_tree_entry_type(entry) != GIT_OBJECT_BLOB)
                return 0;

            const char *name = git_tree_entry_name(entry);
            if (!name) return 0;

            // note: root ends with "/"
            std::string path = root && *root
                ? std::string(root) + name
                : name;

            out->insert(std::move(path));
            return 0;
        },
        &out
    );

    git_tree_free(tree);
    return out;
}

static int diff_cb(
    const git_diff_delta *delta,
    float progress,
    void *payload)
{
    auto *ctx = static_cast<Context *>(payload);

    const git_diff_file *f = (
        delta->new_file.path ? &delta->new_file
        : &delta->old_file
    );

    if (!f->path) return 0;

    const char *path = f->path;

    const git_diff_file *oldf = &delta->old_file;
    const git_diff_file *newf = &delta->new_file;

    bool has_old = oldf->path && oldf->path[0];
    bool has_new = newf->path && newf->path[0];

    if (DEBUG) {
        // debug
        std::cerr << "path=" << path
            << " commit=" << git_oid_tostr_s(ctx->oid)
            << " time=" << ctx->time
            << " status=" << delta->status
            << " old=" << (delta->old_file.path ?: "")
            << " new=" << (delta->new_file.path ?: "")
            << " old_size=" << delta->old_file.size
            << " new_size=" << delta->new_file.size
            << " is_rename=" << ((delta->status == GIT_DELTA_RENAMED) ? "1" : "0")
            << " is_remaining=" << ctx->remaining.count(path)
            << " is_seen=" << ctx->seen.count(path)
            << "\n";
    }

    if (delta->status == GIT_DELTA_DELETED) {
        // this is confusing, because path is in ctx->remaining
        // because path is present in the HEAD tree
        // and there is no "add" commit between the "delete" commit and HEAD
        // so we resolve this contradiction by ignoring the next "add" commit
        ctx->ignore_next_add.emplace(path);
        return 0;
    }

    if (delta->status == GIT_DELTA_ADDED && ctx->ignore_next_add.count(path)) {
        ctx->ignore_next_add.erase(path);
        return 0;
    }

    if (!has_old && has_new) {
        return 0;
    }

    if (has_old && !has_new)
        return 0;

    if (!has_old && !has_new) // unreachable?
        return 0;

    // this requires git_diff_find_similar
    if (delta->status == GIT_DELTA_RENAMED)
        return 0;

    if (
        // path is part of the HEAD tree
        ctx->remaining.count(path) &&
        // path has not been processed
        !ctx->seen.count(path)
    ) {
        ctx->seen[path] = ctx->time;
        ctx->remaining.erase(path);
        ctx->files_found++;
    }

    return 0;
}

void print_stats(Context &ctx)
{
    using namespace std::chrono;

    auto now = steady_clock::now();
    double elapsed = duration_cast<duration<double>>(now - ctx.start_time).count();
    double since_last = duration_cast<duration<double>>(now - ctx.last_print_time).count();

    if (since_last < 0.5) return; // throttle output (2 Hz max)

    ctx.last_print_time = now;

    size_t remaining = ctx.remaining.size();
    size_t total = ctx.files_found + remaining;

    double commits_per_sec = ctx.commits / (elapsed + 1e-9);
    double files_per_sec = ctx.files_found / (elapsed + 1e-9);
    double progress = total ? (1.0 * ctx.files_found / total) : 0.0;

    double eta = (1 - progress) * total / files_per_sec;

    std::cerr
        << "stats: "
        << "commits=" << ctx.commits
        << " time=" << elapsed
        << " eta=" << eta
        << " commits/s=" << commits_per_sec
        << " files_done=" << ctx.files_found
        << " files_left=" << remaining
        << " files/s=" << files_per_sec
        << " progress=" << (progress * 100.0) << "%\n";
}

int main() {
    git_libgit2_init();

    git_repository *repo = nullptr;
    git_revwalk *walk = nullptr;

    if (git_repository_open(&repo, ".") != 0) {
        std::cerr << "failed to open repo\n";
        return 1;
    }

    git_revwalk_new(&walk, repo);

    git_revwalk_push_head(walk);

    git_revwalk_sorting(walk, GIT_SORT_TOPOLOGICAL);

    auto ctx = std::make_unique<Context>();

    ctx->start_time = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    ctx->last_print_time = ctx->start_time;

    ctx->remaining = collect_head_tree(repo);

    git_oid oid;

    while (!git_revwalk_next(&oid, walk)) {

        ctx->commits++;

        if (ctx->commits % PRINT_STATS_EVERY_N_COMMITS == 0) {
            print_stats(*ctx);
        }

        // std::cerr << "commit: " << git_oid_tostr_s(&oid) << "\n"; // debug

        git_commit *commit;
        git_commit_lookup(&commit, repo, &oid);

        // skip merge commits
        if (git_commit_parentcount(commit) > 1)
            continue;

        git_time_t t = git_commit_time(commit);

        git_tree *tree;
        git_commit_tree(&tree, commit);
```

6/13/2026, 7:43:30 AM

The falling commits/s is actually a very strong clue.

Your algorithm is:

1.  Walk every commit.
2.  For every commit, compute a tree diff against parent.
3.  For every changed path, do:
    ``` cpp
    ctx->remaining.count(path)
    ctx->seen.count(path)
    ```

At the beginning, `remaining` contains ~52k files.

After 100k commits, it still contains ~16k files.

So the hash lookups should actually get *faster*, not slower.

The slowdown is almost certainly somewhere else.

# Suspect 1: massive memory leak

I immediately notice:

``` cpp
git_commit *commit;
git_commit_lookup(&commit, repo, &oid);

...

git_tree *tree;
git_commit_tree(&tree, commit);

...

git_tree *parent_tree = nullptr;

...

git_commit_parent(&parent, commit, 0);
git_commit_tree(&parent_tree, parent);

...

git_diff *diff = nullptr;
git_diff_tree_to_tree(&diff, repo, parent_tree, tree, &opts);
```

but I never see:

``` cpp
git_diff_free(diff);
git_tree_free(tree);
git_tree_free(parent_tree);
git_commit_free(commit);
```

inside the loop.

That alone would explain:

- RAM grows to 2 GB
- runtime gets worse over time
- cache pressure increases
- allocator gets slower

You are allocating millions of libgit2 objects and never releasing them.

I would expect RAM usage to stay roughly constant.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Suspect 2: you're diffing entire trees

This is the real killer.

Every commit does:

``` cpp
git_diff_tree_to_tree(...)
```

For nixpkgs.

Every.

Single.

Commit.

Even when only one file changed.

libgit2 must recursively compare trees to discover changed files.

This is O(tree size).

On nixpkgs that's huge.

So your algorithm is approximately:

``` text
number_of_commits × tree_size
```

which is horrible.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Suspect 3: no early exit

You already have:

``` cpp
ctx->remaining
```

When it becomes empty you should stop.

But I don't see:

``` cpp
if (ctx->remaining.empty())
    break;
```

inside the revwalk.

For nixpkgs maybe it never becomes empty, but on many repos it will.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Better stats

Your current commits/s is averaged since program start:

``` cpp
commits_per_sec = ctx.commits / elapsed;
```

That hides what's really happening.

Instead print instantaneous speed.

Store:

``` cpp
size_t last_commits = 0;
size_t last_files = 0;
```

and:

``` cpp
double dt = now - last_print;

double cps =
    (ctx.commits - last_commits) / dt;

double fps =
    (ctx.files_found - last_files) / dt;
```

This will immediately show where the slowdown starts.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Biggest optimization available

You currently do:

``` cpp
commit
  -> build diff
     -> inspect paths
```

for every commit.

The opposite direction is faster:

``` text
HEAD tree
    ↓
blob oid
    ↓
find first commit introducing current blob
```

because identical blobs occur everywhere.

For nixpkgs there are only a few hundred thousand unique blobs but \>100k commits.

This is the "blob ancestry" algorithm we discussed earlier.

Its complexity is closer to:

``` text
changed blobs
```

instead of:

``` text
commits × tree size
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Why commits/s falls from 8 to 3

My bet:

90% probability it's the leaked libgit2 objects.

The evidence:

``` text
start:
8.9 commits/s

end:
3.1 commits/s

RAM:
~2GB
```

That pattern screams:

``` text
more allocations
→ larger working set
→ cache misses
→ slower allocator
→ lower throughput
```

Before changing the algorithm, I'd first add:

``` cpp
git_diff_free(diff);

if (parent_tree)
    git_tree_free(parent_tree);

git_tree_free(tree);
git_commit_free(commit);
```

at the end of every loop iteration and rerun on nixpkgs.

I would not be surprised if that alone gets you back near constant throughput and cuts RAM from ~2 GB to something like tens of MB.

## Response:

6/13/2026, 7:50:26 AM

No, not in any meaningful way.

For code like:

``` cpp
while (...) {
    git_commit *commit;
    git_tree *tree;
    git_tree *parent_tree = nullptr;

    ...
}
```

the variables themselves live on the stack. Creating them is basically free. The compiler usually turns this into a fixed stack frame that is reused for every iteration.

Moving them outside:

``` cpp
git_commit *commit = nullptr;
git_tree *tree = nullptr;
git_tree *parent_tree = nullptr;

while (...) {
    ...
}
```

does **not** avoid any libgit2 allocations. The expensive operations are:

``` cpp
git_commit_lookup(...)
git_commit_tree(...)
git_commit_parent(...)
git_commit_tree(...)
git_diff_tree_to_tree(...)
```

Those allocate internal libgit2 objects and perform object database lookups.

The pointer variables are just 8-byte addresses.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

What *will* help is making sure you free everything every iteration.

I notice your loop currently leaks quite a lot:

``` cpp
git_commit_lookup(&commit, repo, &oid);

git_commit_tree(&tree, commit);

...

git_diff_tree_to_tree(&diff, repo, parent_tree, tree, &opts);

git_diff_foreach(...);
```

but I don't see:

``` cpp
git_diff_free(diff);
git_tree_free(tree);
git_tree_free(parent_tree);
git_commit_free(commit);
```

inside the loop.

If those are really missing, then the 2 GB RAM growth is simply a leak.

For a repo the size of nixpkgs, leaking one commit/tree/diff per iteration will absolutely grow into gigabytes.

At the end of every iteration you should have something like:

``` cpp
git_diff_free(diff);

if (parent_tree)
    git_tree_free(parent_tree);

git_tree_free(tree);
git_commit_free(commit);
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Another thing:

``` cpp
ctx->seen[path] = ctx->time;
```

copies the entire path string.

With 50k+ files that's not terrible, but you're storing:

``` cpp
remaining  // unordered_set<string>
seen       // unordered_map<string,time>
```

which means every path exists twice.

Memory could be cut roughly in half by changing the algorithm to:

``` cpp
unordered_map<string, git_time_t> result;
```

and removing entries from `remaining` without duplicating them into `seen`.

Or even:

``` cpp
unordered_map<string, BlobState>
```

where each path exists only once.

But 50k paths should be tens of MB, not 2 GB.

A 2 GB footprint strongly suggests leaked libgit2 objects or huge diff structures being retained.

I'd inspect that first. If you add the missing frees and RAM still climbs steadily, then we should look at `git_diff_tree_to_tree()` and whether libgit2 is internally accumulating caches.

## Response:

6/13/2026, 12:20:14 PM

What you're seeing is actually exactly what I'd expect from the current algorithm.

The reason is not that old commits are slower to read.

The reason is that your algorithm does **more work per commit as you go deeper into history**.

Right now, for every commit, you're doing:

``` cpp
git_commit_lookup(...)
git_commit_tree(...)
git_commit_parent(...)
git_commit_tree(...)
git_diff_tree_to_tree(...)
git_diff_foreach(...)
```

The expensive step is:

``` cpp
git_diff_tree_to_tree(parent_tree, tree)
```

because libgit2 must recursively compare two trees.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Look at your statistics:

At commit 1000:

``` text
files_left=51730
```

At commit 100000:

``` text
files_left=15897
```

You have already resolved ~70% of files.

Yet you're still diffing every commit.

So most of the runtime near the end is spent discovering:

``` text
"Nope, none of the remaining files changed here either."
```

over and over.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The huge clue is this:

``` text
commits/s:
8.9
8.5
7.0
5.0
3.3
```

A commit object is tiny.

Reading 100k commits from a packfile should not slow down 3x.

The thing that changes is tree size.

As you go back in nixpkgs history, the repo gets reorganized constantly.

Old commits often have enormous tree differences.

`git_diff_tree_to_tree()` becomes more expensive.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

You can verify this immediately.

Add counters:

``` cpp
size_t deltas_seen = 0;
```

inside `diff_cb`:

``` cpp
ctx->deltas_seen++;
```

and print

``` cpp
deltas_per_commit =
    ctx->deltas_seen / double(ctx->commits);
```

I suspect you'll see that the average number of deltas per commit keeps growing.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The bigger issue is architectural.

You're still solving:

``` text
for commit in history:
    diff(commit,parent)
```

This is O(history).

For nixpkgs:

``` text
100k commits
50k files
```

and you're paying for 100k diffs.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The optimization you mentioned:

> skip trees if we have processed all files in a tree

is actually the right direction.

Git trees already form a hierarchy:

``` text
pkgs/
lib/
nixos/
maintainers/
...
```

Suppose:

``` text
pkgs/foo/bar.nix
pkgs/foo/baz.nix
pkgs/foo/qux.nix
```

all have already been resolved.

Then when traversing history:

``` text
tree oid for pkgs/foo
```

becomes irrelevant.

If a subtree contains no unresolved HEAD files:

``` cpp
remaining_in_subtree == 0
```

you never need to descend into it again.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

This leads to a much faster algorithm.

Instead of:

``` text
commit diff
```

do:

``` text
HEAD tree
    recursively walk backwards
```

using tree OIDs.

For each directory subtree:

``` cpp
(head_tree_oid, historical_tree_oid)
```

If the OIDs match:

``` cpp
return;
```

Entire subtree unchanged.

No parsing.

No recursion.

No blob lookups.

No diffs.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

This is essentially what Git itself does internally.

Tree OIDs are Merkle hashes.

If two tree OIDs are equal:

``` text
every file below is identical
```

for free.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

For nixpkgs this is enormous.

Most commits touch:

``` text
1-20 files
```

out of:

``` text
50,000+
```

files.

Meaning:

``` text
99.9% of tree OIDs
```

remain unchanged.

A tree-OID-pruning algorithm skips almost everything.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Another thing:

Your current code uses:

``` cpp
git_revwalk_sorting(walk, GIT_SORT_TOPOLOGICAL);
```

Topological order is not cache-friendly.

For this workload I'd try:

``` cpp
git_revwalk_sorting(
    walk,
    GIT_SORT_TIME
);
```

or

``` cpp
GIT_SORT_TIME | GIT_SORT_REVERSE
```

depending on traversal direction.

Packfiles are often arranged roughly chronologically.

You may get noticeably better locality.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The biggest performance gain, though, is probably eliminating `git_diff_tree_to_tree()` entirely.

That function is extremely general.

You don't actually want a diff.

You want:

``` text
for each unresolved HEAD blob:
    find newest commit that changed it
```

A specialized tree-OID walk can be orders of magnitude faster because it exploits the fact that you're only interested in files currently in HEAD and can prune entire subtrees once all files under them are resolved.

That's the direction I'd pursue next rather than multiprocessing. Multiprocessing won't help much if every worker is still spending most of its time constructing huge tree diffs.

You're now heading toward the right algorithm.

The key insight is:

> You don't care about paths.  
> You don't care about diffs.  
> You care about the blobs currently reachable from HEAD and when they last changed.

That means `git_diff_tree_to_tree()` is doing vastly more work than necessary.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## First simplification: track blobs, not paths

Suppose HEAD contains

    path1 -> blob A
    path2 -> blob B
    path3 -> blob C

Initialize:

``` cpp
remaining_blobs = {A, B, C};
```

Then walk commits backwards.

For each commit:

    tree(commit)
    tree(parent)

Compare trees recursively.

Whenever you discover:

    blob A exists in commit
    blob A absent in parent

then:

    last_change[A] = commit_time
    remaining_blobs.erase(A)

because you've found the commit that introduced the current version of blob A.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## But renames?

Renames disappear automatically.

Example:

    HEAD

    foo.txt -> blob X

History:

    commit3: rename bar.txt -> foo.txt
    commit2: bar.txt -> blob X
    commit1: ...

Blob X never changes.

Walking backwards:

    commit3:
    foo.txt disappears
    bar.txt appears
    blob X exists both sides

No change.

Exactly what you want.

No rename detection required.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Even better: compare blob IDs only

You don't need content diffs.

You only need:

``` cpp
git_tree_entry_id(entry)
```

which is the blob OID.

If blob OID unchanged:

    file contents unchanged

because Git blobs are content-addressed.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Tree pruning

This is where the huge speedup comes from.

Suppose a subtree:

    pkgs/

has tree hash

    abcd1234

in commit N.

Later you see another commit where

    pkgs/

has the exact same tree hash.

Then:

``` text
every file
every blob
every subdirectory
inside pkgs/
is identical
```

No need to descend.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Pseudo:

``` cpp
unordered_set<git_oid> seen_trees;
```

Recursive compare:

``` cpp
compare_tree(parent_tree, tree)
{
    if (git_oid_equal(
        git_tree_id(parent_tree),
        git_tree_id(tree)))
        return;

    ...
}
```

Actually that's enough for parent-child comparison.

You don't even need a global cache yet.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## More aggressive pruning

Keep:

``` cpp
unordered_set<git_oid> finished_trees;
```

meaning:

> every HEAD blob inside this tree has already been resolved.

Then:

``` cpp
if (finished_trees.contains(tree_oid))
    return;
```

This can eliminate enormous portions of history.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Memory concern

You are correct.

For nixpkgs:

    ~100k commits
    millions of distinct tree objects

A global

``` cpp
unordered_set<git_oid>
```

for every tree ever seen

could easily reach hundreds of MB.

Each entry roughly:

    20 bytes oid
    + allocator
    + hash table overhead
    ≈ 40-60 bytes

A few million trees:

    100-300 MB

or more.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Better cache

Only cache trees that matter.

Example:

``` cpp
struct TreeState {
    bool finished;
};

unordered_map<git_oid, TreeState>
```

Insert only when:

- tree contains at least one HEAD blob
- or subtree becomes fully resolved

This stays much smaller.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# The really big optimization

You actually don't need to walk all commits.

Think about what you're looking for.

For blob X in HEAD:

    find first commit backwards where
    blob X differs from parent

That's essentially a reachability problem.

Git already has machinery for this:

    git blame
    git log --follow
    pickaxe

But for 50k files that becomes expensive too.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# What I'd try next

Replace

``` cpp
git_diff_tree_to_tree()
```

with a custom recursive tree comparison:

``` cpp
compare_tree(parent, current)
```

that:

1.  compares entry names
2.  compares entry OIDs
3.  descends only into changed subtrees
4.  only cares about blobs currently in `remaining_blobs`

This alone is likely a **10×–100× speedup** over full diff generation.

The reason is that `git_diff_tree_to_tree()` is building a complete diff of every changed path in every commit, while you only care about a tiny subset of blobs from HEAD.

The fact that `GIT_SORT_NONE` already took you from ~4 commits/s to ~50 commits/s suggests most of your runtime is framework overhead, not actual object decompression. A specialized tree walker should give another large jump.
